title: CPU and MMU
what: The memory management unit is the part of each CPU core that translates every virtual address an instruction uses into a physical address before the access reaches the caches and RAM. It walks the page tables in hardware, starting from a root register (CR3 on x86-64, TTBR0/TTBR1 on arm64, satp on RISC-V), and raises a page fault when an entry is missing or forbids the access.
why: Programs need private, stable addresses that do not depend on where their data sits in RAM, and the kernel needs to stop one program touching another's memory. Doing that check in software on every load and store would be far too slow, so it is done by dedicated hardware.
varies: The translation format depends on the architecture, the base page size and the configured virtual address width: x86-64 uses 4 levels and 48-bit addresses, or 5 levels and 57 bits with LA57; arm64 offers 4, 16 and 64 KiB granules with 39 to 52 bits; RISC-V offers Sv39, Sv48 and Sv57. Inside a virtual machine a second stage of translation, controlled by the hypervisor, follows the one the guest sees.

title: Translation lookaside buffer
what: The TLB is a small cache inside the MMU that holds recently used translations, from virtual page to physical frame together with the permissions. A hit translates an address with no memory reads at all; a miss costs a page-table walk of up to one read per level.
why: Without it every memory access would need several further memory accesses just to find out where to go. Because programs touch the same pages repeatedly, a few thousand entries satisfy almost every access.
varies: Its reach is the number of entries times the page size, so huge pages (2 MiB or 1 GiB on x86-64) multiply the memory one entry covers. When the kernel changes a mapping it must invalidate stale entries, on other CPUs too (a TLB shootdown); address-space identifiers such as PCID or ASID let entries of several processes coexist across context switches.

title: CPU caches
what: Caches are small, fast memories between the cores and RAM, organised in levels: a private L1 and usually L2 per core, and a larger L3 shared by many cores. They hold memory in fixed-size lines, typically 64 bytes, addressed by physical address.
why: RAM takes on the order of a hundred nanoseconds to answer, hundreds of instructions' worth of time. Keeping recently and nearby used data close to the core hides most of that latency.
varies: Sizes, associativity and which CPUs share a level differ by model; virtual machines often report incomplete or invented cache information.

title: CPU topology
what: The nest of packages, dies, cores and hardware threads a machine is built from, as firmware describes it and the kernel publishes it in /sys/devices/system/cpu. Each hardware thread is a logical CPU, the unit the scheduler places tasks on; sibling threads share one core's execution units and caches.
why: Where a task runs decides what it shares: two tasks on sibling threads compete for one core, a task moved to another package leaves its cached data behind, and on hybrid processors some cores are faster than others. The scheduler builds its domains from this nest.
varies: Desktop x86 parts usually run two threads per core; many arm boards and most virtual machines one. Hybrid processors mix performance and efficiency cores. Inside a virtual machine the topology is whatever the hypervisor presents.

title: Frequency scaling (cpufreq)
what: The kernel subsystem that sets how fast each group of CPUs runs. A policy covers the CPUs that share a clock; a driver (intel_pstate, amd-pstate, acpi-cpufreq, cpufreq-dt) talks to the hardware; a governor (schedutil, performance, powersave) decides, usually from how busy the scheduler says the CPUs are.
why: Power grows faster than linearly with frequency, so running fast only when there is work saves energy and heat, and turbo frequencies can only be sustained on a few cores at a time.
varies: Hardware-managed drivers let the CPU choose within limits and an energy-performance preference; virtual machines usually have no cpufreq at all, because the hypervisor owns the frequency.

title: Run queues
what: Every CPU has a run queue holding the tasks that are ready to run there, sorted by scheduling class. A task that sleeps leaves the queue; a task that wakes is placed on one; load balancing moves tasks between queues. The load average, procs_running and the run-queue wait time in /proc/schedstat all describe these queues.
why: One queue per CPU lets each CPU pick its next task without a global lock, at the cost of having to balance the queues against each other.
varies: A busy server shows long waits and a load average near or above its CPU count; a desktop mostly idle queues. Inside a container, the load average and schedstat describe the host's queues.

title: Fair scheduler (EEVDF, formerly CFS)
what: The scheduling class of ordinary tasks. It shares each CPU in proportion to weights set by nice values, tracking each task's virtual runtime; since Linux 6.6 it runs the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline (EEVDF), before that the one with the smallest virtual runtime (CFS). Real-time and deadline classes run before it; sched_ext can replace its policy with a BPF program.
why: Most work has no deadline but should neither starve nor hog the CPU; weighted fair sharing gives every runnable task a predictable share and bounded latency.
varies: Kernels before 6.6 use CFS; 6.12 and later can load a sched_ext scheduler. Autogroup and cgroup weights share CPU between groups before tasks.

title: CPU cgroup controllers
what: The cpu controller shares CPU time between groups of processes by weight (cpu.weight) and caps it with a quota per period (cpu.max), throttling a group that has used its quota until the next period; the cpuset controller restricts which CPUs a group may run on. Containers and systemd slices use both.
why: A quota keeps one tenant from taking a whole machine even when it is idle otherwise, and a CPU set keeps latency-sensitive work away from the rest.
varies: cgroup v1 named the quota cpu.cfs_quota_us and the weight cpu.shares. A container's quota is invisible to nproc and to /proc/cpuinfo, which still show every CPU.

title: Page tables
what: Page tables are the radix tree, one per address space, that maps each virtual page to a physical frame. The kernel writes them; the MMU reads them. Each level is one page of 8-byte entries indexed by a slice of the virtual address, and a leaf entry can sit above the last level to map a huge page.
why: A flat table for a 48-bit address space would need 512 GiB per process. A tree only needs tables for the parts of the address space that are actually mapped, and a missing entry is how the kernel defers work until a page is touched.
varies: The number of levels and the bits per level follow the paging format; a process that maps more memory, or maps it sparsely, needs more page-table pages, which meminfo reports as PageTables and each process's status file as VmPTE.

title: Physical frames
what: A frame is one page-sized, page-aligned piece of RAM, the unit the kernel hands out. Each has a descriptor (struct page, grouped into folios) of about 64 bytes recording who uses it. MemTotal is the number of frames the kernel manages, after firmware and the kernel itself have taken what they need.
why: Managing RAM in fixed-size units makes allocation and translation simple: any free frame can back any virtual page. The descriptors are how the kernel finds which processes map a frame and whether it can be reclaimed.
varies: Firmware reservations, the kernel image, the descriptor array, a crash kernel and integrated graphics all shrink MemTotal below the installed RAM by amounts that differ between machines. In a VM the frames are what the hypervisor presents, and may be backed by host swap.

title: NUMA nodes
what: A NUMA node is a set of CPUs together with the memory attached closest to them. On a multi-socket or chiplet machine, memory on a CPU's own node is faster to reach than memory on another node. The kernel keeps separate free lists, zones and reclaim threads for each node.
why: Attaching all memory to one shared bus does not scale to many cores, so large machines give each group of cores its own memory controller. The kernel must then know which memory is near which CPU to place pages well.
varies: Most laptops and desktops have one node; servers have one per socket or more. Firmware decides what is reported, and a VM may see one node on a multi-node host or invented nodes on a single-node one.

title: Memory zones
what: Each node's frames are divided into zones by physical address range: DMA and DMA32 for devices that can only reach low addresses, Normal for everything else, and Movable, which holds only pages the kernel can migrate, so that the memory can be emptied for unplugging or compaction. Each zone has min, low and high watermarks, the allocator's own definition of running short.
why: Some devices cannot address all of RAM, so the kernel must keep memory they can use available. The watermarks decide when background reclaim starts, when allocations must reclaim for themselves, and when only emergency allocations may proceed.
varies: Which zones exist depends on the architecture and the amount of RAM: 64-bit machines with little memory may have no Normal zone above DMA32. Watermarks scale with min_free_kbytes and watermark_scale_factor and with each zone's size.

title: Buddy allocator
what: The page allocator keeps each zone's free memory in lists of blocks of 2^order contiguous frames. A request takes a block of the right order, splitting a larger one if needed; a freed block merges with its free neighbour, its buddy, into a larger block. /proc/buddyinfo counts the free blocks of each order.
why: Most allocations need one frame, but transparent huge pages, kernel stacks, some drivers and DMA buffers need physically contiguous runs. Splitting and merging power-of-two blocks finds those runs cheaply and keeps free memory as unfragmented as allocations allow.
varies: After long uptime with mixed workloads free memory fragments into small blocks, so large-order requests fail or trigger compaction even when plenty is free. Per-CPU free lists in front of the buddy lists make single-frame allocations faster and hold some free frames out of the counts.

title: Process address space
what: Each process has its own virtual address space (mm_struct): one page-table tree plus the list of mappings that say what belongs at each address. Threads of a process share it. The kernel's own memory is mapped into the upper part of every address space but is inaccessible from user mode.
why: Separate address spaces isolate programs from each other and let every program be linked as if it had the machine to itself. Reserving address space costs nothing until it is used, so programs can map far more than there is RAM.
varies: Address space layout randomisation (randomize_va_space) moves the stack, heap, libraries and executable between runs. The size of the user range follows the paging format, and limits such as max_map_count and RLIMIT_AS can cap a process.

title: Virtual memory areas
what: A VMA (vm_area_struct) records one mapping: an address range, its permissions, whether it is private or shared, and what backs it, a file and offset or nothing (anonymous). Each line of /proc/<pid>/maps is one VMA. The kernel indexes them in a maple tree (a red-black tree before Linux 6.1).
why: The kernel must know what should be at an address before anything is there, so that it can supply the page on first touch, check permissions, and know where to read it back from after reclaim.
varies: A typical process has tens to thousands of VMAs; mprotect or munmap in the middle of one splits it, adjacent compatible ones merge. max_map_count caps their number per process.

title: Page fault handler
what: When the MMU finds no valid translation for an access it raises a page fault, and the kernel's handler runs with the faulting address. It finds the VMA (none, or wrong permissions, means SIGSEGV), then supplies the page: a zeroed frame or the shared zero page for anonymous memory, the cached file page, a copy for copy-on-write, or the page read back from swap.
why: Faults are how the kernel keeps the promises that mmap made only when they are called in, so memory that is never touched never costs a frame. A fault that had to wait for I/O is a major fault; the rest are minor.
varies: Transparent huge pages let one anonymous fault map 2 MiB, and fault-around maps up to 16 neighbouring file pages at once, so fault counts are usually lower than page counts. Major faults are usually file reads; swap-ins are major faults too.

title: Anonymous memory
what: Anonymous pages have no file behind them: heaps, stacks and private mappings that have been written. Their only copy is in RAM, so the only way to free their frames without losing data is to write them to swap.
why: Programs need scratch memory that starts zeroed and belongs to them alone. Backing it with no file keeps it cheap, at the price of making it hard to reclaim.
varies: With THP enabled, anonymous memory may be mapped in 2 MiB pages (AnonHugePages). Without swap, anonymous memory cannot be reclaimed at all, which shifts all memory pressure onto the page cache.

title: Page cache
what: The page cache holds the contents of files in RAM, one cache per file indexed by offset. read() copies from it, mmap maps its pages directly, and writes modify it and are written back to storage later. Cached in meminfo is its size, including shared memory.
why: Storage is thousands of times slower than RAM, and an idle frame does no work, so the kernel keeps file data after use until something needs the memory. Clean cache can be dropped instantly, which is why it counts as available.
varies: On a machine that has read many files the cache fills most of free memory, and MemFree is small while MemAvailable stays large. Writeback timing follows dirty_ratio, dirty_background_ratio and dirty age; tmpfs files live in the cache but cannot be dropped.

title: Shared memory and tmpfs
what: shmem is memory that looks like a file but has no disk behind it: tmpfs files, /dev/shm, memfd_create, shared anonymous mappings and System V shared memory. It is counted in Cached and Shmem, but like anonymous memory it can only be reclaimed to swap.
why: Processes need memory they can share by name or file descriptor, and temporary files that never need to reach disk. Implementing them as files in the page cache gives one mechanism for mapping, sharing and accounting.
varies: Its size depends on what uses /dev/shm, tmpfs mounts such as /tmp, and graphics buffers; without swap none of it can be reclaimed, even though it appears in the cache figures.

title: LRU lists and reclaim
what: Reclaim frees frames by choosing pages that are unlikely to be needed soon: dropping clean file pages, writing back dirty ones, and swapping out anonymous ones. Pages are ranked on least-recently-used lists, either the classic active and inactive pair per type or the generations of Multi-Gen LRU.
why: The kernel fills memory on purpose, so allocations can only keep succeeding if something continually takes frames back. Choosing badly evicts pages that are immediately faulted back in, which the kernel detects as refaults.
varies: swappiness sets the relative cost of reclaiming anonymous versus file pages; without swap only file pages can be reclaimed. Kernels from 6.1 can use Multi-Gen LRU, which ages memory by scanning page tables rather than lists.

title: kswapd
what: kswapd is the per-node kernel thread that reclaims in the background. It wakes when a zone falls below its low watermark and works until the zone is above its high watermark. If memory falls to the min watermark first, the allocating task must reclaim for itself, which is called direct reclaim and makes it stall.
why: Reclaiming ahead of demand keeps most allocations fast; direct reclaim is the fallback when background reclaim cannot keep up, and its stalls are what users feel as a slow machine.
varies: A quiet machine shows few kswapd scans; a machine under pressure shows growing pgscan_direct and allocstall counts and non-zero memory pressure stall figures.

title: Swap areas
what: A swap area is a partition, a file or a zram device where the kernel writes anonymous and shmem pages it reclaims, so their frames can be reused. Areas have priorities; a swapped page is read back by a major fault on next touch, often with neighbours (page-cluster).
why: Without somewhere to put them, anonymous pages can never leave RAM, however long they go untouched. Swap lets cold anonymous memory make room for cache and active work.
varies: Many machines run without swap, some with a disk partition or file, some with only compressed swap in RAM. Swap in use does not mean the machine is short of memory now: pages stay in swap until touched.

title: zswap and zram
what: zswap compresses pages on their way to swap and keeps them in a RAM pool; pages reach the real swap device when zswap refuses them (pool at its limit, or poorly compressible) or writes cold ones back, on hitting its limit or, with its shrinker enabled, under memory pressure. zram is a block device whose contents are compressed in RAM, commonly used as the only swap area.
why: Compressing a page is much faster than writing it to storage, and typical memory compresses to about half its size, so swapping to compressed RAM gains capacity at a modest CPU cost.
varies: Some distributions enable zram swap by default, others zswap, others neither. A zram device's size is its uncompressed capacity, not the RAM it uses.

title: OOM killer
what: When an allocation cannot be satisfied even after reclaim and compaction, the kernel's out-of-memory killer chooses a process, normally the one using the most memory adjusted by oom_score_adj, and kills it. The OOM reaper then frees its memory quickly.
why: The kernel promises more memory than exists (overcommit), so when the promises are called in at once something must give. Killing one process is the alternative to failing allocations that kernel code cannot handle.
varies: The overcommit mode decides how much is promised. Memory cgroups have their own OOM killer acting at the cgroup limit, and user-space daemons such as systemd-oomd often act earlier, on pressure stall information.

title: Memory cgroup
what: A memory cgroup accounts the memory of a group of processes and can limit it: memory.high throttles and reclaims above a soft boundary, memory.max triggers reclaim and then an OOM kill inside the group. Containers and systemd slices are built on them.
why: System-wide limits cannot stop one service starving the others. Accounting and reclaiming per group lets a machine be shared with predictable limits.
varies: Under cgroup v2 the limits live in memory.max and memory.high; cgroup v1 used different files. A container can be OOM-killed at its limit while the host has plenty free.

title: Request queues and I/O schedulers
what: The multi-queue block layer (blk-mq) stages requests in a software queue per CPU and dispatches them to one or more hardware queues per device, each mapped to a set of CPUs. An I/O scheduler (none, mq-deadline, bfq or kyber) may sit between the two, holding and reordering requests; writeback throttling limits how many background writes are in flight.
why: One lock-protected queue per device could not keep up with flash serving hundreds of thousands of operations per second from many CPUs; a scheduler still pays off where the order of requests matters, on spinning disks and slow flash, or where processes must get fair shares.
varies: NVMe drives usually have a hardware queue per CPU and run without a scheduler; SATA disks, SD cards and many virtual disks have one queue and get mq-deadline by default; distributions and administrators choose bfq for slow devices. Device-mapper and md volumes have no queue of their own.

title: Block devices
what: A block device presents storage as an array of 512-byte sectors that can be read, written, flushed and discarded in any order: disks, partitions, device-mapper volumes, loop devices and zram. The block layer turns bios into requests, splitting and merging them to the device's limits, and counts every completed request.
why: Filesystems and swap need a uniform interface regardless of whether the storage is NVMe, SATA, an SD card, a network volume or compressed RAM.
varies: Logical and physical block sizes, the largest request, the volatile write cache and discard support come from the device; rotational disks make random access slow, and virtual disks often report themselves as rotational whatever backs them. Inside a container /sys/block lists the host's devices.

title: Writeback and backing devices
what: Flusher threads write dirty page cache pages back to their device, one writeback context per backing device (BDI): every few seconds for data older than the expiry age, at once when dirty data passes the background threshold, and on fsync, sync or reclaim. balance_dirty_pages slows tasks that dirty pages faster than their device writes them, and each BDI has its own share of the dirty limit.
why: Deferring writes lets programs continue at memory speed and lets the kernel combine and order them, but dirty data is lost in a crash and occupies memory, so its amount and age must be bounded and its writers held to the device's pace.
varies: The thresholds follow vm.dirty_ratio and vm.dirty_background_ratio, or the _bytes variants, against the memory that is free or file cache; a slow device gets a small share of the limit; FUSE filesystems use a strict per-device limit; cgroup v2 accounts writeback to the cgroup that dirtied the pages.

instances.title: {name}: up to {max_ratio}% of the dirty limit

title: Filesystems
what: A filesystem organises a block device, or nothing at all for virtual ones such as tmpfs and procfs, into files and directories, and the mount table joins them into one tree. The virtual filesystem layer (VFS) gives them one interface of superblocks, inodes, dentries and open files; file data passes through the page cache on its way in and out, and a journal or copy-on-write keeps the on-disk structure consistent across crashes.
why: Programs need named, durable, shareable data; the VFS lets every filesystem plug into the same system calls and the same page cache, so programs need not care which one they use.
varies: Which filesystems are mounted, and with which options (the access-time policy, journaling mode, commit interval, compression), depends on the distribution and the administrator; a container sees its own mount tree, usually with overlay at its root.

title: The probe process
what: The probe is a short-lived child process Machine Atlas starts during collection. It makes five mappings with known histories (untouched, written and read anonymous memory, a private file mapping, a shared memfd), then lets the parent read its /proc files, so lessons can show how the kernel accounts memory whose use is known exactly.
why: Other processes' memory maps are private, and the system-wide figures mix everything together. A process whose actions are known turns the kernel's accounting into an experiment with a known answer.
varies: Results depend on THP availability, fragmentation and the kernel version; with --no-probe, or in a snapshot made without it, these values are not collected.

title: Network interface controllers
what: A network interface controller moves frames between the wire or the radio and RAM. The driver gives it rings of descriptors pointing at buffers; the NIC transmits from and receives into them by DMA, then raises an interrupt. Modern NICs have many queue pairs, hash incoming flows across them (RSS), compute checksums and split large segments into frames themselves (TSO).
why: Copying every byte through the CPU, one interrupt per packet, cannot keep up with links of tens of gigabits per second. Rings, DMA, several queues and offloads let the hardware work in batches and in parallel with the CPUs.
varies: A laptop has one queue per direction or a handful; a server NIC has one per CPU. Wireless NICs report no fixed link speed, virtual NICs (virtio, veth) report what the hypervisor or nothing, and a container sees no hardware at all.

title: Network interfaces
what: A network interface (struct net_device) is the kernel's handle for anything that sends and receives packets: a hardware NIC, the loopback device, a bridge, a bond of several NICs, one end of a veth pair, a tunnel. Each has a type, an MTU, an operational state, transmit queues and its own addresses.
why: The rest of the stack routes, queues and counts packets per interface without knowing whether a cable, a radio, another namespace or a VPN process is behind it.
varies: Names follow udev's predictable scheme (enp3s0, wlp4s0) or the driver's (eth0, wlan0). Containers see only their own veth end and lo; hosts of containers grow bridges and veths; servers bond NICs for bandwidth and redundancy.

title: Routing tables
what: The routing tables map destination prefixes to an interface and, for destinations not on a directly attached network, a gateway. For each packet without a cached decision the kernel takes the most specific matching prefix, preferring the lowest metric among equals; policy rules choose which table to consult.
why: A machine attached to several networks needs a rule for where each packet leaves, and a default for everything else.
varies: A desktop has a default route and a few connected networks; a container host adds one per bridge; a VPN may route everything through a tunnel, sometimes from a separate table that /proc/net/route does not show.

title: Connection tracking
what: Netfilter calls hooks at fixed points of the packet path (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting). Connection tracking, the nf_conntrack module, uses them to follow every flow in a table, so firewall rules can say "established" and NAT can rewrite the replies of a connection it rewrote.
why: Stateless packet filters cannot tell a reply from an unsolicited packet, and address translation needs to remember each mapping.
varies: Loaded only when some rule needs it: Docker's NAT and most firewalls do, a bare machine may not. A busy server can fill the table, after which new flows are dropped.

title: Receive processing (NAPI)
what: When a NIC signals received packets, its driver disables the interrupt and schedules a NAPI poll; the network receive softirq then pulls packets from the ring in batches, up to a budget, merges segments (GRO) and passes them up the stack on that CPU. Packets steered between CPUs (RPS) or from devices without NAPI wait in a per-CPU backlog.
why: An interrupt per packet would drown the CPU at high rates; polling in batches only while there is work keeps latency low when idle and throughput high under load.
varies: softnet_stat shows how the work spreads: one CPU on a simple NIC without RPS, all CPUs on a multiqueue server NIC. Drops there mean the backlog overflowed; squeezes mean the budget ran out.

title: Queueing disciplines
what: A queueing discipline (qdisc) holds the packets waiting to leave through an interface and decides their order: a simple FIFO with priority bands (pfifo_fast), fair queues per flow with active queue management (fq_codel), per-flow pacing (fq), or one child qdisc per hardware queue (mq). Virtual devices usually have none (noqueue).
why: Packets arrive in bursts faster than a link drains them. Where they wait, and how many may wait, decides both throughput and how much latency a bulk transfer adds to everything else.
varies: Distributions choose the default (net.core.default_qdisc), usually fq_codel; servers running BBR often choose fq; older systems keep pfifo_fast. Multiqueue NICs get mq with one child per queue.

title: TCP
what: The kernel's TCP implementation turns a socket's byte stream into numbered segments, retransmits what is lost, keeps per-connection state through the TCP state machine, sizes its buffers automatically, and paces its sending rate with a congestion control algorithm (cubic, bbr).
why: IP delivers packets without promises: they may be lost, duplicated or reordered. Programs want an ordered, reliable stream that shares the network fairly with others.
varies: The congestion control algorithm, buffer ceilings and queue limits are tunables; distributions differ, and tuned servers raise them. Each network namespace has its own sockets and most TCP settings.

title: Sockets
what: A socket is the file descriptor through which a program uses a protocol: send() and recv() copy data into and out of the socket's send and receive buffers, and the protocol below moves it. TCP, UDP, Unix and netlink sockets share this layer.
why: Programs should not handle packets, retransmissions or routing; they read and write a descriptor, and the kernel does the rest.
varies: A desktop holds hundreds of Unix sockets and a few dozen TCP connections; a server can hold hundreds of thousands. Inside a container only the container's own sockets are visible.
